content:
The Sovereign Gold Bond scheme is gone. Gold in India is trading near Rs. 1.6 lakh per 10 grams today, up roughly 65% in a year. For anyone who relied on SGBs as the clean, government-backed way to own gold, that creates a real gap to fill. Here's what your options look like, what each one actually costs, and whether buying at these prices makes sense.

Key Takeaways

  • The Government of India stopped issuing new SGBs in February 2024. No new tranches are planned.
  • Gold ETFs are now the closest substitute: expense ratio under 0.5%, LTCG at 12.5% after just 12 months.
  • Gold Mutual Funds work the same way but don't require a demat account. SIP from Rs. 500 a month.
  • Digital gold through apps like PhonePe and Google Pay is not SEBI-regulated. Fine under Rs. 50,000, not ideal for larger amounts.
  • Most advisors recommend 10 to 15% of your portfolio in gold. Count your jewellery before buying more.

Why Were Sovereign Gold Bonds So Useful?

SGBs were a genuinely good deal. You got gold price exposure plus a fixed 2.5% annual interest paid by the government, and when the bond matured after 8 years, you paid zero capital gains tax on the price appreciation. No storage hassle, no purity questions. For a patient investor, it was hard to beat.

The discontinuation occured quietly, with no announcement of a replacement scheme. The government's calculation: SGBs had become an expensive form of borrowing, costing more than standard bonds, and physical gold imports hadn't dropped the way the policy intended. Budget 2024-25 closed the door on new issuances.

If you already hold SGBs, keep them until maturity. You'll still get the interest payments and the favourable tax treatment at the end. New investors won't recieve those benefits.

What Are Your Gold Investment Options Now?

Four main options remain: physical gold, Gold ETFs, Gold Mutual Funds, and digital gold. Gold ETFs and Gold Mutual Funds are now the best substitutes for SGBs, with a 12-month LTCG holding period and total annual costs under 1%. Physical gold and digital gold both require 24 months of holding for long-term capital gains treatment.

Here's an honest comparison of all four:

OptionEntry CostNeeds Demat?LTCG PeriodBest For
Physical Gold (coins/bars)2 to 3% premium over marketNo24 monthsThose who want tangibility
Gold ETF (e.g. Nippon Gold BeES)Brokerage only, negligibleYes12 monthsActive investors with demat accounts
Gold Mutual Fund (e.g. HDFC Gold Fund)No entry loadNo12 monthsSIP investors and beginners
Digital Gold (PhonePe, Google Pay)0 to 2.5% spreadNo24 monthsSmall amounts only

The practical difference between a Gold ETF and a Gold Mutual Fund is one layer of fees. A Gold Mutual Fund buys units of a Gold ETF on your behalf and charges a small additional management fee. Gold ETFs are very slightly cheaper. But if you don't already trade stocks, setting up a demat account just for gold isn't worth it. A Gold Mutual Fund is the simpler starting point, and the cost difference for most retail investors is small enough to ignore.

Digital gold looks appealing because you can buy Rs. 10 worth on any app without a demat account. But it isn't regulated by SEBI. There's no investor protection framework comparable to mutual funds. Use it to accumulate small amounts or send as a gift. Don't park serious savings there.

How Is Gold Taxed in India in 2026?

The 2024 Union Budget simplified the rules for listed assets, gold investments included. For Gold ETFs and Gold Mutual Funds, gains from holdings sold after more than 12 months are taxed as long-term capital gains at 12.5% with no indexation. Holdings sold within 12 months are taxed at your applicable slab rate.

Physical gold has a longer threshold: 24 months for LTCG, same 12.5% rate, no indexation. The old system that taxed long-term gold gains at 20% but let you adjust the cost base for inflation is gone for everyone now.

Gold jewellery is definately the most expensive way to hold gold from an investment standpoint. Making charges of 5 to 15% are added at the point of purchase and are non-recoverable on exit. If you're buying jewellery as jewellery, that's fine. As a pure investment strategy, it doesn't work.

Is It a Good Time to Buy Gold at Rs. 1.6 Lakh Per 10 Grams?

Gold has gained roughly 65% in the past 12 months. At Rs. 1.6 lakh per 10 grams, a lump-sum entry is a bet on the rally continuing. For long-term portfolio allocation, a monthly SIP into a Gold Mutual Fund makes more sense than either waiting for a dip or betting everything on today's price.

Say you want to add Rs. 30,000 to your gold allocation this year. Putting it all in today is a pure timing call. Breaking it into Rs. 5,000 monthly SIP installments over six months doesn't guarantee a better average price, but it removes the "did I buy the top" anxiety entirely. That's the practical reason most advisors favour SIPs even at record highs.

One honest caveat: if you're buying gold now primarily because global uncertainty feels high, you're reacting to a news cycle. Central banks have been buying gold aggressively since 2022, which provides a price floor, but the safe-haven premium is already in today's price. A permanent 10 to 15% gold allocation as portfolio insurance is a sound strategy. Buying gold because things feel scary is usually timing a peak, not building a portfolio.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will Sovereign Gold Bonds Start Again in India?

No announcement has been made about resuming the SGB scheme as of September 2026. The government cited high borrowing costs as the reason for discontinuation. Most analysts don't expect a resumption near-term, though the scheme hasn't been formally abolished, so a future restart isn't ruled out permanently.

Can I Buy Gold ETFs Without a Demat Account?

No. Gold ETFs require a demat account and a trading account with a registered broker. If you don't have one, a Gold Mutual Fund is simpler: it invests in Gold ETFs on your behalf, requires only PAN and basic KYC, and lets you start a SIP from Rs. 500 per month with no demat account needed.

Is Digital Gold Safe in India?

Digital gold from platforms like Augmont or MMTC-PAMP is backed by physical gold in vaults, but it isn't regulated by SEBI or RBI. There is no investor protection framework comparable to mutual funds. Fine for amounts under Rs. 50,000, but for larger investments, Gold ETFs or Gold Mutual Funds are the safer choice.

What Happened to the 2.5% Interest on Existing SGBs?

The 2.5% annual interest continues for all SGBs already issued before the scheme was discontinued. Existing holders will keep receiving interest until their bond matures and benefit from zero capital gains tax at maturity. New investors can't access this benefit. No other gold product currently offers a guaranteed annual return on top of price appreciation.

How Much of My Portfolio Should Be in Gold?

Most financial advisors in India recommend 10 to 15% of total invested assets in gold, treating it as a hedge rather than a growth asset. That figure includes the value of gold jewellery you already own. Many Indian households are effectively over 30% in gold once jewellery is counted, which is more than most advisors would recommend.

The Short Version

SGBs are gone, and the best replacement for most investors is a Gold Mutual Fund (no demat needed, SIP from Rs. 500) or a Gold ETF if you already have a trading account. At Rs. 1.6 lakh per 10 grams, a monthly SIP is more sensible than a lump sum. Keep gold to 10 to 15% of your portfolio, and count your jewellery in that figure.

This post is for information only and is not financial advice. For decisions about your own investments, consult a SEBI-registered investment advisor.
